claim: HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers harbor few mutations in the Hippo signaling pathway compared to HPV-negative cancers at the same anatomical site.
source: HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers harbor few mutations in the Hippo signaling pathway compared to HPV-negative cancers at the same anatomical site, prompting the hypothesis that an HPV-encoded protein inactivates the Hippo pathway and activates the Hippo effector yes-associated protein (YAP1).
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis data from TCGA showing differential mutation frequencies between HPV-positive and HPV-negative cancers.

claim: The HPV E7 oncoprotein is required for HPV infection.
source: The HPV E7 oncoprotein is required for HPV infection and for HPV-mediated oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Statement based on established scientific knowledge about HPV biology.

claim: The HPV E7 oncoprotein is required for HPV-mediated oncogenic transformation.
source: The HPV E7 oncoprotein is required for HPV infection and for HPV-mediated oncogenic transformation.
evidence: Statement based on established scientific knowledge about HPV biology.

claim: E7 activates YAP1, promoting YAP1 nuclear localization in basal epithelial cells.
source: We investigated the effects of HPV oncoproteins on YAP1 and found that E7 activates YAP1, promoting YAP1 nuclear localization in basal epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from organotypic cultures shown in Figure 1.

claim: YAP1 activation by HPV E7 required that E7 binds and degrades the tumor suppressor protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 14 (PTPN14).
source: YAP1 activation by HPV E7 required that E7 binds and degrades the tumor suppressor protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 14 (PTPN14).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using E7 mutants that cannot bind PTPN14.

claim: E7 required YAP1 transcriptional activity to extend the lifespan of primary keratinocytes.
source: E7 required YAP1 transcriptional activity to extend the lifespan of primary keratinocytes, indicating that YAP1 activation contributes to E7 carcinogenic activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using TEADi inhibitor shown in Figure 6.

claim: YAP1 activation contributes to E7 carcinogenic activity.
source: E7 required YAP1 transcriptional activity to extend the lifespan of primary keratinocytes, indicating that YAP1 activation contributes to E7 carcinogenic activity.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of YAP1 for E7's lifespan-extending activity.

claim: YAP1 activation causes HPV E7 expressing cells to be retained in the basal compartment of stratified epithelia.
source: Maintaining infection in basal cells is critical for HPV persistence, and here we demonstrate that YAP1 activation causes HPV E7 expressing cells to be retained in the basal compartment of stratified epithelia.
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: YAP1 activation resulting from PTPN14 inactivation is an essential, targetable activity of the HPV E7 oncoprotein relevant to HPV infection and carcinogenesis.
source: We propose that YAP1 activation resulting from PTPN14 inactivation is an essential, targetable activity of the HPV E7 oncoprotein relevant to HPV infection and carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is a proposed conclusion based on the experimental findings presented.

claim: Nearly 5% of human cancer cases are caused by persistent infection with one of the high-risk (oncogenic) HPV genotypes.
source: Nearly 5% of human cancer cases are caused by persistent infection with one of the high-risk (oncogenic) HPV genotypes (de Martel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Martel et al., 2020.

claim: High-risk HPV E6 proteins target p53 for proteasome-mediated degradation.
source: Two well-characterized instances of tumor suppressor inactivation by HPV are high-risk HPV E6 proteins targeting p53 for proteasome-mediated degradation and high-risk HPV E7 proteins binding and degrading the retinoblastoma protein (RB1) (Heck et al., 1992; Münger et al., 1989; Scheffner et al., 1990; Werness et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: High-risk HPV E7 proteins bind and degrade the retinoblastoma protein (RB1).
source: Two well-characterized instances of tumor suppressor inactivation by HPV are high-risk HPV E6 proteins targeting p53 for proteasome-mediated degradation and high-risk HPV E7 proteins binding and degrading the retinoblastoma protein (RB1) (Heck et al., 1992; Münger et al., 1989; Scheffner et al., 1990; Werness et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Both p53 degradation and RB1 inactivation are required for productive HPV infection.
source: Both p53 degradation and RB1 inactivation are required for productive HPV infection (Collins et al., 2005; Flores et al., 2000; Kho et al., 2013; McLaughlin-Drubin et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: E7 is essential for HPV-mediated carcinogenesis.
source: In addition to supporting productive infection, E7 is essential for HPV-mediated carcinogenesis (Mirabello et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mirabello et al., 2017.

claim: Genes in the p53 pathway and in the RB1-related cell cycle pathway are frequently mutated in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) but infrequently mutated in HPV-positive HNSCC.
source: The impact of the HPV oncoproteins on cell growth control pathways is reflected in human cancer genomic data: genes in the p53 pathway and in the RB1-related cell cycle pathway are frequently mutated in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) but infrequently mutated in HPV-positive HNSCC (Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018 and genomic data analysis.

claim: RB1 binding/degradation by high-risk HPV E7 is necessary but insufficient for E7 transforming activity.
source: RB1 binding/degradation by high-risk HPV E7 is necessary but insufficient for E7 transforming activity (Balsitis et al., 2006; Balsitis et al., 2005; Banks et al., 1990; Ciccolini et al., 1994; Helt and Galloway, 2001; Huh et al., 2005; Ibaraki et al., 1993; Jewers et al., 1992; Phelps et al., 1992; Strati and Lambert, 2007; White et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The Hippo signaling pathway is more frequently mutated in HPV-negative than in HPV-positive HNSCC.
source: Human cancer genomic data indicates that like the p53 and cell cycle pathways, the Hippo signaling pathway is more frequently mutated in HPV-negative than in HPV-positive HNSCC.
evidence: Supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When the Hippo kinases are inactive, YAP1 and TAZ are activated and translocate to the nucleus.
source: The core Hippo pathway consists of a kinase cascade upstream of the effector proteins yes-associated protein (YAP1) and its paralog transcriptional coactivator with PDZ binding motif (TAZ). When the Hippo kinases are inactive, YAP1 and TAZ are activated and translocate to the nucleus.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of Hippo pathway biology.

claim: In stratified squamous epithelia, YAP1 is primarily expressed in the basal layer.
source: In stratified squamous epithelia, YAP1 is primarily expressed in the basal layer, where YAP1 activation is regulated by contextual cues including cell density, tension in the extracellular matrix, and contact with the basement membrane (Elbediwy et al., 2016; Totaro et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: YAP1 activation is regulated by contextual cues including cell density, tension in the extracellular matrix, and contact with the basement membrane.
source: In stratified squamous epithelia, YAP1 is primarily expressed in the basal layer, where YAP1 activation is regulated by contextual cues including cell density, tension in the extracellular matrix, and contact with the basement membrane (Elbediwy et al., 2016; Totaro et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: In normal stratified squamous epithelia, activation of YAP1 and TAZ promotes expansion of the basal cell compartment.
source: In normal stratified squamous epithelia, activation of YAP1 and TAZ promotes expansion of the basal cell compartment and inhibition of YAP1 and TAZ allows keratinocytes to differentiate (Beverdam et al., 2013; Elbediwy and Thompson, 2018; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Totaro et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Inhibition of YAP1 and TAZ allows keratinocytes to differentiate.
source: In normal stratified squamous epithelia, activation of YAP1 and TAZ promotes expansion of the basal cell compartment and inhibition of YAP1 and TAZ allows keratinocytes to differentiate (Beverdam et al., 2013; Elbediwy and Thompson, 2018; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Totaro et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Mutations in many of the tumor suppressors upstream of YAP1/TAZ are common in a variety of cancer types.
source: Mutations in many of the tumor suppressors upstream of YAP1/TAZ are common in a variety of cancer types (Moroishi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moroishi et al., 2015.

claim: PTPN14 has been implicated as a tumor suppressor and negative regulator of YAP1.
source: Protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 14 (PTPN14) has been implicated as a tumor suppressor and negative regulator of YAP1 (Knight et al., 2018; Mello et al., 2017; Poernbacher et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: E7 proteins from diverse HPV genotypes bind directly to PTPN14 and recruit the E3 ligase UBR4 to direct PTPN14 for proteasome-mediated degradation.
source: E7 proteins from diverse HPV genotypes bind directly to PTPN14 and recruit the E3 ligase UBR4 to direct PTPN14 for proteasome-mediated degradation (Szalmás et al., 2017; White et al., 2016; White et al., 2012b; Yun et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: PTPN14 degradation and RB1 binding/degradation are separable activities of HPV E7 that each contributes to E7 carcinogenic activity.
source: We have shown that PTPN14 degradation and RB1 binding/degradation are separable activities of HPV E7 that each contributes to E7 carcinogenic activity (Hatterschide et al., 2020; Hatterschide et al., 2019; White et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: PTPN14 inactivation in human keratinocytes does not cause an increase in canonical YAP1 target genes CTGF and CYR61.
source: However, the downstream consequences of PTPN14 degradation are poorly understood, and so far we have not observed that PTPN14 inactivation in human keratinocytes causes an increase in canonical YAP1 target genes CTGF and CYR61.
evidence: Based on previous observations by the authors.

claim: Expression of high-risk HPV E7 is sufficient to activate YAP1.
source: Here we show that expression of high-risk HPV E7 is sufficient to activate YAP1 and that HPV E7 requires YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity to promote cell growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: HPV E7 requires YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity to promote cell growth.
source: Here we show that expression of high-risk HPV E7 is sufficient to activate YAP1 and that HPV E7 requires YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity to promote cell growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: HPV E7 must bind PTPN14 to activate YAP1.
source: We demonstrate that HPV E7 must bind PTPN14 to activate YAP1 and that PTPN14 inactivation alone is sufficient to activate YAP1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using E7 mutants shown in Figure 2.

claim: PTPN14 inactivation alone is sufficient to activate YAP1.
source: We demonstrate that HPV E7 must bind PTPN14 to activate YAP1 and that PTPN14 inactivation alone is sufficient to activate YAP1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using PTPN14 knockout cells shown in Figure 2.

claim: YAP1 activation by HPV E7 is restricted to the basal layer of the epithelium.
source: YAP1 activation by HPV E7 is restricted to the basal layer of the epithelium where we found PTPN14 expression to be enriched.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: PTPN14 expression is enriched in the basal layer of the epithelium.
source: YAP1 activation by HPV E7 is restricted to the basal layer of the epithelium where we found PTPN14 expression to be enriched.
evidence: Supported by laser capture microdissection and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HPV infection begins in basal epithelial keratinocytes.
source: HPV infection begins in basal epithelial keratinocytes (Day and Schelhaas, 2014; Pyeon et al., 2009; Roberts et al., 2007) and infected basal cells are the site of persistent HPV infection (Doorbar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Infected basal cells are the site of persistent HPV infection.
source: HPV infection begins in basal epithelial keratinocytes (Day and Schelhaas, 2014; Pyeon et al., 2009; Roberts et al., 2007) and infected basal cells are the site of persistent HPV infection (Doorbar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doorbar et al., 2021.

claim: The basal cell compartment contains the only long-lived cells in the epithelium.
source: The basal cell compartment contains the only long-lived cells in the epithelium and the HPV genome can be maintained in dividing cells in a largely dormant state (Egawa et al., 2012; Parish et al., 2006; You et al., 2004).
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of epithelial biology.

claim: The HPV genome can be maintained in dividing cells in a largely dormant state.
source: The basal cell compartment contains the only long-lived cells in the epithelium and the HPV genome can be maintained in dividing cells in a largely dormant state (Egawa et al., 2012; Parish et al., 2006; You et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Activation of YAP1 and TAZ has been proposed to maintain the progenitor cell state in several different epithelia.
source: Activation of YAP1 and TAZ has been proposed to maintain the progenitor cell state in several different epithelia (Beverdam et al., 2013; Heng et al., 2020; Hicks-Berthet et al., 2021; Szymaniak et al., 2015; Yimlamai et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: YAP1 activation and PTPN14 degradation by E7 both promote the maintenance of cells in the basal compartment of stratified epithelia.
source: Testing this hypothesis, we found that YAP1 activation and PTPN14 degradation by E7 both promote the maintenance of cells in the basal compartment of stratified epithelia.
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: YAP1 activation facilitates HPV persistence and contributes to the carcinogenic activity of high-risk HPV E7.
source: We propose that YAP1 activation facilitates HPV persistence and contributes to the carcinogenic activity of high-risk HPV E7.
evidence: This is a proposed conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The cell cycle, p53, and Hippo pathways are the three pathways that exhibit the greatest difference in alteration frequency in HPV-negative vs HPV-positive HNSCC.
source: A comprehensive analysis of somatic mutations and copy number variations in human tumor samples revealed that the cell cycle, p53, and Hippo pathways are the three pathways that exhibit the greatest difference in alteration frequency in HPV-negative vs HPV-positive HNSCC (Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018 and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: HPV-negative OPSCC were more frequently altered in the p53, cell cycle, and Hippo pathways than HPV-positive OPSCC.
source: Consistent with previous findings, HPV-negative OPSCC were more frequently altered in the p53, cell cycle, and Hippo pathways than HPV-positive OPSCC.
evidence: Supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hippo pathway alterations in HPV-negative HNSCC or OPSCC include amplification of the YAP1/TAZ oncogenes or inactivating mutations in one or more of the upstream inhibitors of YAP1/TAZ, including PTPN14.
source: Hippo pathway alterations in HPV-negative HNSCC or OPSCC include amplification of the YAP1/TAZ oncogenes or inactivating mutations in one or more of the upstream inhibitors of YAP1/TAZ, including PTPN14.
evidence: Based on analysis of genomic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Organotypic cultures of primary human foreskin keratinocytes (HFK) harboring an HPV18 genome exhibited increased YAP1 staining and increased YAP1 nuclear localization in the basal layer of the epithelium compared to HFK cultures.
source: Organotypic cultures of primary human foreskin keratinocytes (HFK) harboring an HPV18 genome exhibited increased YAP1 staining and increased YAP1 nuclear localization, indicative of YAP1 activation, in the basal layer of the epithelium compared to HFK cultures (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PCNA transcription increases upon RB1 inactivation and is a marker of HPV E7 expression.
source: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) transcription increases upon RB1 inactivation and is a marker of HPV E7 expression (Cheng et al., 1995; Flores et al., 2000; Lee et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: YAP1 activation in the HPV18 genome containing cells was restricted to the basal cells, while PCNA levels were elevated in both the basal and suprabasal layers of the epithelium.
source: Although YAP1 activation in the HPV18 genome containing cells was restricted to the basal cells, PCNA levels were elevated in both the basal and suprabasal layers of the epithelium in the same cultures.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: YAP1 expression and nuclear localization were increased in the HPV16 E7 and HPV18 E7 expressing cells relative to parental HFK.
source: YAP1 expression and nuclear localization were increased in the HPV16 E7 and HPV18 E7 expressing cells relative to parental HFK (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A-C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: YAP1 nuclear localization increased modestly in organotypic cultures of HPV16 E6 expressing cells.
source: YAP1 nuclear localization increased modestly in organotypic cultures of HPV16 E6 expressing cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A-C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Constitutive expression of either HPV16 E7 or HPV18 E7 induced PCNA expression in basal and suprabasal cells.
source: Constitutive expression of either HPV16 E7 or HPV18 E7 induced PCNA expression in basal and suprabasal cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: HPV promotes increased YAP1 expression and nuclear localization in basal keratinocytes.
source: We conclude that HPV promotes increased YAP1 expression and nuclear localization in basal keratinocytes and that E7 is sufficient for YAP1 activation.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from organotypic cultures.

claim: E7 is sufficient for YAP1 activation.
source: We conclude that HPV promotes increased YAP1 expression and nuclear localization in basal keratinocytes and that E7 is sufficient for YAP1 activation.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from organotypic cultures.

claim: YAP1 levels and YAP1 nuclear localization were increased in PTPN14 KO cultures compared to controls.
source: We found that YAP1 levels and YAP1 nuclear localization were increased in PTPN14 KO cultures compared to controls (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: YAP1 activation in basal epithelial cells lacking PTPN14 was comparable to YAP1 activation in HPV E7 cells.
source: YAP1 activation in basal epithelial cells lacking PTPN14 was comparable to YAP1 activation in HPV E7 cells.
evidence: Based on comparison of immunofluorescence data from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Loss of PTPN14 expression activates YAP1 in basal keratinocytes.
source: We conclude that loss of PTPN14 expression activates YAP1 in basal keratinocytes.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from PTPN14 knockout organotypic cultures.

claim: The HPV18 E7 R84S variant is unable to bind or degrade PTPN14.
source: A highly conserved C-terminal arginine in E7 makes a direct interaction with the C-terminus of PTPN14 and the HPV18 E7 R84S variant is unable to bind or degrade PTPN14 (Hatterschide et al., 2020; Yun et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: YAP1 expression and nuclear localization in the basal layer of HPV18 E7 R84S cultures were reduced compared to HPV18 E7 WT controls.
source: Indeed, YAP1 expression and nuclear localization in the basal layer of HPV18 E7 R84S cultures were reduced compared to HPV18 E7 WT controls (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 5A-C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PTPN14 loss increased basal cell density from an average of 5.5 cells per 100 μm in control cultures to 9.0 cells per 100 μm in PTPN14 KO cultures.
source: In addition to activating YAP1, PTPN14 loss increased basal cell density from an average of 5.5 cells per 100 μm in control cultures to 9.0 cells per 100 μm in PTPN14 KO cultures (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Basal cell density was higher in HPV18 E7 WT cultures (9.4 cells per 100 μm) than in HPV18 E7 R84S cultures (7.1 cells per 100 μm).
source: Basal cell density was higher in HPV18 E7 WT cultures (9.4 cells per 100 μm) than in HPV18 E7 R84S cultures (7.1 cells per 100 μm) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No statistically significant difference in suprabasal cell density was observed in either comparison.
source: No statistically significant difference in suprabasal cell density was observed in either comparison (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: E7 expression or PTPN14 loss in stratified squamous epithelia is sufficient to activate YAP1 in the basal layer of the epithelium and increase basal cell density.
source: We conclude that E7 expression or PTPN14 loss in stratified squamous epithelia is sufficient to activate YAP1 in the basal layer of the epithelium and increase basal cell density.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from organotypic cultures.

claim: In a single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of human neonatal foreskin epidermis, PTPN14 mRNA expression was enriched in the basal-III cluster.
source: In a recent single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of human neonatal foreskin epidermis, PTPN14 mRNA expression was enriched in the basal-III cluster (Figure 3A and B; Wang et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of published single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The basal-III cell cluster was described to be nonproliferating, marked by COL17A1 expression, and predicted to differentiate directly into spinous cells based on pseudotime analysis.
source: The basal-III cell cluster was described to be nonproliferating, marked by COL17A1 expression, and predicted to differentiate directly into spinous cells based on pseudotime analysis.
evidence: Based on characterization from the cited single-cell RNA-seq study.

claim: PTPN14 expression was higher in basal-III cells than in the spinous or granular cell clusters.
source: PTPN14 expression was higher in basal-III cells than in the spinous or granular cell clusters.
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was an approximately fivefold enrichment of PTPN14 mRNA in the basal epithelial layer compared to the suprabasal layers.
source: We found that there was an approximately fivefold enrichment of PTPN14 mRNA in the basal epithelial layer compared to the suprabasal layers (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by laser capture microdissection and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The basal integrins ITGA6 and ITGB4 were expressed in the basal layer.
source: As expected, the basal integrins ITGA6 and ITGB4 were expressed in the basal layer (Figure 3E) and the differentiation markers KRT1 and IVL were expressed in the suprabasal layers (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from laser capture microdissection shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The differentiation markers KRT1 and IVL were expressed in the suprabasal layers.
source: As expected, the basal integrins ITGA6 and ITGB4 were expressed in the basal layer (Figure 3E) and the differentiation markers KRT1 and IVL were expressed in the suprabasal layers (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from laser capture microdissection shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The same pattern of PTPN14 mRNA expression was observed in an organotypic culture grown from primary HFK expressing HPV18 E7 WT.
source: The same pattern of PTPN14 mRNA expression was observed in an organotypic culture grown from primary HFK expressing HPV18 E7 WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PTPN14 mRNA is enriched in basal keratinocytes in the presence or absence of HPV E7.
source: We conclude that PTPN14 mRNA is enriched in basal keratinocytes in the presence or absence of HPV E7.
evidence: Conclusion based on laser capture microdissection and qRT-PCR data.

claim: PTPN14 acts as a YAP1 inhibitor specifically in the basal compartment of stratified epithelia.
source: Our data support that PTPN14 acts as a YAP1 inhibitor specifically in the basal compartment of stratified epithelia.
evidence: Conclusion based on the basal-specific expression of PTPN14 and YAP1 activation patterns.

claim: The primary effect of PTPN14 inactivation on transcription is to repress epithelial differentiation gene expression.
source: In previous unbiased experiments we found that the primary effect of PTPN14 inactivation on transcription is to repress epithelial differentiation gene expression (Hatterschide et al., 2020; Hatterschide et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on previous published work by the authors.

claim: PTPN14 inactivation did not increase expression of the canonical YAP1/TAZ targets CTGF and CYR61.
source: However, we also observed that PTPN14 inactivation did not increase expression of the canonical YAP1/TAZ targets CTGF and CYR61.
evidence: Based on previous observations by the authors.

claim: There was minimal overlap between PTPN14-dependent differentially expressed genes and the genes listed in the MSigDB conserved YAP1 signature.
source: Consistent with this difference there was minimal overlap between PTPN14-dependent differentially expressed genes and the genes listed in the MSigDB conserved YAP1 signature (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Transduction of keratinocytes with a PTPN14 lentivirus induced the expression of the differentiation markers KRT10 and IVL in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Transduction of keratinocytes with a PTPN14 lentivirus induced the expression of the differentiation markers KRT10 and IVL in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: HFK transfected with control siRNA exhibited the expected increase in KRT1 and IVL after transduction with PTPN14 lentivirus.
source: HFK transfected with control siRNA exhibited the expected increase in KRT1 and IVL after transduction with PTPN14 lentivirus (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Keratinocytes depleted of YAP1/TAZ did not express relatively more KRT1 or IVL when PTPN14 was overexpressed than when it was not.
source: However, keratinocytes depleted of YAP1/TAZ did not express relatively more KRT1 or IVL when PTPN14 was overexpressed than when it was not.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: PTPN14 requires YAP1 and/or TAZ to regulate differentiation gene expression in keratinocytes.
source: We conclude that PTPN14 requires YAP1 and/or TAZ to regulate differentiation gene expression in keratinocytes.
evidence: Conclusion based on siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: Both pairs of YAP1/TAZ siRNA had the same effect on differentiation in response to PTPN14 overexpression yet only one pair efficiently depleted TAZ protein levels.
source: Both pairs of YAP1/TAZ siRNA had the same effect on differentiation in response to PTPN14 overexpression yet only one pair efficiently depleted TAZ protein levels (Figure 4B), leading us to speculate that YAP1 is the key intermediate connecting PTPN14 levels to differentiation gene expression.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: YAP1 is the key intermediate connecting PTPN14 levels to differentiation gene expression.
source: Both pairs of YAP1/TAZ siRNA had the same effect on differentiation in response to PTPN14 overexpression yet only one pair efficiently depleted TAZ protein levels (Figure 4B), leading us to speculate that YAP1 is the key intermediate connecting PTPN14 levels to differentiation gene expression.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential effects of YAP1 vs TAZ knockdown.

claim: Depletion of PTPN14, LATS1, or LATS2 all decreased differentiation gene expression to a similar degree.
source: Depletion of PTPN14, LATS1, or LATS2 all decreased differentiation gene expression to a similar degree.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: None of the three knockdowns (PTPN14, LATS1, or LATS2) significantly affected the levels of CTGF or CYR61.
source: None of the three knockdowns significantly affected the levels of CTGF or CYR61 (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: Direct depletion of YAP1 or WWTR1 affected both differentiation gene expression and CTGF/CYR61 levels.
source: Direct depletion of YAP1 or WWTR1 affected both differentiation gene expression and CTGF/CYR61 levels.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 4E-H.

claim: YAP1 knockdown always had a stronger effect than did WWTR1 knockdown.
source: YAP1 knockdown always had a stronger effect than did WWTR1 knockdown and our qRT-PCR analyses supported that WWTR1 transcript levels were low in HFK.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: WWTR1 transcript levels were low in HFK.
source: YAP1 knockdown always had a stronger effect than did WWTR1 knockdown and our qRT-PCR analyses supported that WWTR1 transcript levels were low in HFK.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Inactivation of three different YAP1 inhibitors dampens differentiation gene expression even in the absence of a differentiation stimulus and does not increase canonical YAP1 target gene expression in keratinocytes.
source: This result shows that inactivation of three different YAP1 inhibitors dampens differentiation gene expression even in the absence of a differentiation stimulus and does not increase canonical YAP1 target gene expression in keratinocytes.
evidence: Conclusion based on siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: PTPN14 knockout or E7 expression reduces differentiation gene expression both in undifferentiated cells and in cells stimulated to differentiate.
source: We have previously observed that PTPN14 knockout or E7 expression reduces differentiation gene expression both in undifferentiated cells and in cells stimulated to differentiate (Hatterschide et al., 2020; Hatterschide et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on previous published work by the authors.

claim: PTPN14 promotes differentiation through inhibition of YAP1/TAZ despite not affecting canonical YAP1/TAZ target genes.
source: Taken together, these data support that PTPN14 promotes differentiation through inhibition of YAP1/TAZ despite not affecting canonical YAP1/TAZ target genes.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: HPV-positive HNSCC have a strong propensity toward poorly differentiated, basaloid histology.
source: HPV-positive HNSCC have a strong propensity toward poorly differentiated, basaloid histology (Mendelsohn et al., 2010; Pai and Westra, 2009), which is reflected in their transcriptional profile (Hatterschide et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Forty-three percent of HPV-negative tumors and 12.5% of HPV-positive tumors stained positive for KRT1.
source: Forty-three percent of HPV-negative tumors and 12.5% of HPV-positive tumors stained positive for KRT1.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Each differentiation marker (KRT1, KRT10, and IVL) was expressed at a lower level in HPV-positive PDX than in HPV-negative PDX.
source: Each differentiation marker was expressed at a lower level in HPV-positive PDX than in HPV-negative PDX (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from PDX samples shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no significant difference in expression of CTGF and CYR61 in HPV-positive vs HPV-negative PDX, although there was a trend toward higher CTGF in the HPV-positive PDX.
source: We found no significant difference in expression of these canonical YAP1/TAZ target genes in HPV-positive vs HPV-negative PDX, although there was a trend toward higher CTGF in the HPV-positive PDX (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from PDX samples shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the transcriptomic analyses, CTGF and CYR61 expression trended higher in the HPV-negative HNSCC.
source: In the transcriptomic analyses, CTGF and CYR61 expression trended higher in the HPV-negative HNSCC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pattern of low expression of differentiation markers and unchanged canonical YAP1/TAZ target gene expression in HPV-positive versus HPV-negative patient samples is consistent with the effects of PTPN14 inactivation in cultured cells.
source: The pattern of low expression of differentiation markers and unchanged canonical YAP1/TAZ target gene expression in HPV-positive versus HPV-negative patient samples is consistent with the effects of PTPN14 inactivation in cultured cells.
evidence: Conclusion based on comparison of patient sample data with cell culture experiments.

claim: High-risk but not low-risk HPV E7 proteins can extend the lifespan of primary keratinocytes.
source: High-risk but not low-risk HPV E7 proteins can extend the lifespan of primary keratinocytes (Halbert et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Halbert et al., 1991.

claim: The TEADi protein is a genetically encoded competitive inhibitor that prevents binding between YAP1/TAZ and TEAD transcription factors.
source: The TEADi protein is a genetically encoded competitive inhibitor that prevents binding between YAP1/TAZ and TEAD transcription factors (Yuan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yuan et al., 2020.

claim: HPV16 E7 or HPV18 E7 extended the lifespan of primary HFK based on cumulative population doublings.
source: As anticipated, HPV16 E7 or HPV18 E7 extended the lifespan of primary HFK based on cumulative population doublings (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan extension assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: TEADi induction upon doxycycline treatment decreased the lifespan of primary HFK in the presence or absence of E7.
source: TEADi induction upon doxycycline treatment decreased the lifespan of primary HFK in the presence or absence of E7, but the effect of YAP1/TAZ-TEAD inhibition was greater in the HPV16 E7 and HPV18 E7 cells, where E7 had minimal ability to promote growth in the presence of TEADi.
evidence: Supported by lifespan extension assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The effect of YAP1/TAZ-TEAD inhibition was greater in the HPV16 E7 and HPV18 E7 cells, where E7 had minimal ability to promote growth in the presence of TEADi.
source: TEADi induction upon doxycycline treatment decreased the lifespan of primary HFK in the presence or absence of E7, but the effect of YAP1/TAZ-TEAD inhibition was greater in the HPV16 E7 and HPV18 E7 cells, where E7 had minimal ability to promote growth in the presence of TEADi.
evidence: Supported by lifespan extension assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: High-risk HPV E7 proteins require YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity for their lifespan extending capacity in primary keratinocytes.
source: We conclude that high-risk HPV E7 proteins require YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity for their lifespan extending capacity in primary keratinocytes.
evidence: Conclusion based on TEADi inhibitor experiments.

claim: YAP1 overexpression impairs differentiation and promotes progenitor cell identity in squamous and nonsquamous epithelia.
source: YAP1 overexpression impairs differentiation and promotes progenitor cell identity in squamous and nonsquamous epithelia.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: HPV infection is maintained in a reservoir of infected basal cells and productive virus replication begins upon commitment to differentiation.
source: HPV infection is maintained in a reservoir of infected basal cells and productive virus replication begins upon commitment to differentiation.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of HPV biology.

claim: About 20% of uninduced GFP+ cells were found in the basal layer.
source: In organotypic cultures grown from a 1:25 mixture of GFP-labeled cells and unmodified HFK, about 20% of uninduced GFP+ cells were found in the basal layer.
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Induction of YAP1 WT or YAP1 S127A expression was sufficient to promote the retention of nearly 60% of labeled cells in the basal layer of the epithelium.
source: Induction of YAP1 WT or YAP1 S127A expression was sufficient to promote the retention of nearly 60% of labeled cells in the basal layer of the epithelium (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Only around 40% of GFP+ cells were found in the basal layer when YAP1 S94A was induced.
source: Only around 40% of GFP+ cells were found in the basal layer when YAP1 S94A was induced.
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: YAP1 activation causes cells to be retained in the basal layer of a stratified squamous epithelium.
source: These data indicate that YAP1 activation causes cells to be retained in the basal layer of a stratified squamous epithelium.
evidence: Conclusion based on cell fate monitoring experiments.

claim: The ability of YAP1 to bind TEAD transcription factors contributed to its activity in the cell fate assay.
source: The ability of YAP1 to bind TEAD transcription factors contributed to its activity in the cell fate assay.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced activity of YAP1 S94A mutant that cannot bind TEAD.

claim: 60%–70% of PTPN14 KO tracer cells were found in the basal layer when either of two PTPN14 guide RNAs were used whereas about 20% of control tracer cells were retained in the basal layer.
source: 60%–70% of PTPN14 KO tracer cells were found in the basal layer when either of two PTPN14 guide RNAs were used whereas about 20% of control tracer cells were retained in the basal layer (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: PTPN14 knockout is sufficient to promote basal cell fate determination in keratinocytes.
source: Thus, PTPN14 knockout is sufficient to promote basal cell fate determination in keratinocytes.
evidence: Conclusion based on cell fate monitoring experiments.

claim: Nearly 80% of GFP-labeled HPV18 E7 WT tracer cells were retained in the basal layer compared to about 10% of labeled control cells.
source: We found that nearly 80% of GFP-labeled HPV18 E7 WT tracer cells were retained in the basal layer compared to about 10% of labeled control cells (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: HPV18 E7 WT labeled cells were numerous and grouped in clusters in the basal layer, suggesting that E7 promoted the clonal expansion of labeled basal cells.
source: HPV18 E7 WT labeled cells were numerous and grouped in clusters in the basal layer, suggesting that E7 promoted the clonal expansion of labeled basal cells.
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence images and inference about clonal expansion.

claim: Labeled HPV18 E7 R84S cells exhibited varying degrees of basal cell expansion and basal cell retention and approximately 60% of labeled cells were in the basal layer.
source: Both effects were dampened in experiments using HPV18 E7 R84S tracer cells (cannot degrade PTPN14). Labeled HPV18 E7 R84S cells exhibited varying degrees of basal cell expansion and basal cell retention and approximately 60% of labeled cells were in the basal layer.
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: HPV18 E7 R84S retains the ability to inactivate RB1.
source: HPV18 E7 R84S retains the ability to inactivate RB1 and we interpret these data to mean that the proliferation of labeled basal cells resulted from RB1 inactivation.
evidence: Based on known properties of the R84S mutant.

claim: The proliferation of labeled basal cells resulted from RB1 inactivation.
source: HPV18 E7 R84S retains the ability to inactivate RB1 and we interpret these data to mean that the proliferation of labeled basal cells resulted from RB1 inactivation.
evidence: Interpretation of the cell fate monitoring data.

claim: HPV18 E7 ∆DLLC cannot bind RB1 but can bind and degrade PTPN14.
source: Finally, HPV18 E7 ∆DLLC cannot bind RB1 but can bind and degrade PTPN14.
evidence: Based on known properties of the ∆DLLC mutant.

claim: In a cell fate experiment using GFP-labeled HPV18 E7 ∆DLLC tracer cells, the labeled cells were present mainly as single cells in the basal layer.
source: In a cell fate experiment using GFP-labeled HPV18 E7 ∆DLLC tracer cells, the labeled cells were present mainly as single cells in the basal layer (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-B).
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The behavior of the two mutant HPV E7 proteins supports that PTPN14 degradation is required for basal cell retention and RB1 inactivation is required for basal cell expansion.
source: The behavior of the two mutant HPV E7 proteins supports that PTPN14 degradation is required for basal cell retention and RB1 inactivation is required for basal cell expansion.
evidence: Conclusion based on comparison of E7 mutant behaviors in cell fate assays.

claim: PTPN14 degradation and YAP1 activation by HPV18 E7 promote basal cell retention.
source: We conclude that PTPN14 degradation and YAP1 activation by HPV18 E7 promote basal cell retention.
evidence: Conclusion based on cell fate monitoring experiments.

claim: YAP1 and TAZ are oncogenes that promote growth and inhibit differentiation in stratified squamous epithelia.
source: YAP1 and TAZ are oncogenes that promote growth and inhibit differentiation in stratified squamous epithelia (Elbediwy et al., 2016; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011; Totaro et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: HPV E7 activates YAP1.
source: Here we report that HPV E7 activates YAP1 (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity is required for the carcinogenic activity of HPV E7.
source: YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity is required for the carcinogenic activity of HPV E7 (Figure 6) and YAP1 activation by E7 biases HPV E7-expressing cells to be retained in the basal epithelial layer (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: YAP1 activation by E7 biases HPV E7-expressing cells to be retained in the basal epithelial layer.
source: YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity is required for the carcinogenic activity of HPV E7 (Figure 6) and YAP1 activation by E7 biases HPV E7-expressing cells to be retained in the basal epithelial layer (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: YAP1 activation by HPV E7 enables HPV-infected cells to persist in stratified epithelia.
source: Based on these findings we propose that YAP1 activation by HPV E7 enables HPV-infected cells to persist in stratified epithelia.
evidence: This is a proposed conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: YAP1 activation cooperates with RB1 inactivation to enable the transforming activity of HPV E7.
source: We propose that YAP1 activation cooperates with RB1 inactivation to enable the transforming activity of HPV E7.
evidence: This is a proposed conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: PTPN14 binding by HPV18 E7 was required for activation of YAP1 in the basal layer.
source: PTPN14 binding by HPV18 E7 was required for activation of YAP1 in the basal layer and PTPN14 KO was sufficient for the same effect (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PTPN14 KO was sufficient for activation of YAP1 in the basal layer.
source: PTPN14 binding by HPV18 E7 was required for activation of YAP1 in the basal layer and PTPN14 KO was sufficient for the same effect (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Highly conserved amino acids in E7 participate in binding to PTPN14, indicating that YAP1 activation and maintenance of basal cell state is likely shared among diverse papillomavirus E7 proteins.
source: Highly conserved amino acids in E7 participate in binding to PTPN14 (Hatterschide et al., 2020; Yun et al., 2019), indicating that YAP1 activation and maintenance of basal cell state is likely shared among diverse papillomavirus E7 proteins.
evidence: Inference based on conservation of PTPN14-binding residues.

claim: HPV18 E7 depletes PTPN14 protein levels more efficiently than HPV16 E7.
source: HPV18 E7 depletes PTPN14 protein levels more efficiently than HPV16 E7 (Hatterschide et al., 2020; White et al., 2016), which is consistent with the observed stronger effect of HPV18 E7 on YAP1 nuclear localization in basal cells (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HPV18 E7 has a stronger effect on YAP1 nuclear localization in basal cells than HPV16 E7.
source: HPV18 E7 depletes PTPN14 protein levels more efficiently than HPV16 E7 (Hatterschide et al., 2020; White et al., 2016), which is consistent with the observed stronger effect of HPV18 E7 on YAP1 nuclear localization in basal cells (Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of immunofluorescence data in Figure 1.

claim: Other reports have suggested that HPV might activate YAP1.
source: Although other reports have suggested that HPV might activate YAP1 (He et al., 2015; Morgan et al., 2020; Olmedo-Nieva et al., 2020; Webb Strickland et al., 2018), no specific activity of an HPV protein has previously been shown to enable YAP1 activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to other published research.

claim: No specific activity of an HPV protein has previously been shown to enable YAP1 activation.
source: Although other reports have suggested that HPV might activate YAP1 (He et al., 2015; Morgan et al., 2020; Olmedo-Nieva et al., 2020; Webb Strickland et al., 2018), no specific activity of an HPV protein has previously been shown to enable YAP1 activation.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current findings.

claim: Other groups have proposed that HPV E6 activates YAP1.
source: Other groups have proposed that HPV E6 activates YAP1 (He et al., 2015; Webb Strickland et al., 2018), and we observed modest YAP1 activation by HPV E6 compared to E7.
evidence: Supported by citations to other published research.

claim: We observed modest YAP1 activation by HPV E6 compared to E7.
source: Other groups have proposed that HPV E6 activates YAP1 (He et al., 2015; Webb Strickland et al., 2018), and we observed modest YAP1 activation by HPV E6 compared to E7.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Activation of YAP1 by HPV E7 is contingent upon its ability to bind and degrade PTPN14.
source: We conclude that activation of YAP1 by HPV E7 is contingent upon its ability to bind and degrade PTPN14.
evidence: Conclusion based on experiments with E7 mutants.

claim: Even when HPV E7 was expressed in all layers of a stratified epithelium, YAP1 levels and nuclear localization increased only in basal epithelial cells.
source: Even when HPV E7 was expressed in all layers of a stratified epithelium, YAP1 levels and nuclear localization increased only in basal epithelial cells.
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: E7 required PTPN14 degradation to activate YAP1.
source: We found that E7 required PTPN14 degradation to activate YAP1 and that PTPN14 was expressed predominantly in basal keratinocytes (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: PTPN14 was expressed predominantly in basal keratinocytes.
source: We found that E7 required PTPN14 degradation to activate YAP1 and that PTPN14 was expressed predominantly in basal keratinocytes (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Basal cell-specific expression of PTPN14 is consistent with the observation that it is regulated by p63, the master regulator of basal cell identity in stratified epithelia.
source: Basal cell-specific expression of PTPN14 is consistent with the observation that it is regulated by p63, the master regulator of basal cell identity in stratified epithelia (Perez et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perez et al., 2007.

claim: PTPN14 inhibits YAP1 primarily in basal cells.
source: We propose that PTPN14 inhibits YAP1 primarily in basal cells and that unlike the effects of E7 on RB1 in both differentiated and undifferentiated cells, E7 activates YAP1 primarily in basal cells.
evidence: Proposed conclusion based on the basal-specific expression of PTPN14 and YAP1 activation patterns.

claim: Unlike the effects of E7 on RB1 in both differentiated and undifferentiated cells, E7 activates YAP1 primarily in basal cells.
source: We propose that PTPN14 inhibits YAP1 primarily in basal cells and that unlike the effects of E7 on RB1 in both differentiated and undifferentiated cells, E7 activates YAP1 primarily in basal cells.
evidence: Proposed conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: Degradation of PTPN14 by HPV E7 represses keratinocyte differentiation but does not induce canonical Hippo pathway target genes.
source: Degradation of PTPN14 by HPV E7 represses keratinocyte differentiation but does not induce canonical Hippo pathway target genes (Hatterschide et al., 2020; Hatterschide et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on previous published work by the authors.

claim: PTPN14 overexpression required YAP1/TAZ to promote differentiation gene expression.
source: Nonetheless, we found that PTPN14 overexpression required YAP1/TAZ to promote differentiation gene expression (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Few studies have tested how YAP1 inhibitor inactivation alters gene expression downstream of YAP1.
source: Few studies have tested how YAP1 inhibitor inactivation alters gene expression downstream of YAP1.
evidence: Statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Inactivation of LATS1 or LATS2 decreased expression of differentiation genes in unstimulated cells but did not induce canonical YAP1/TAZ targets.
source: Here we demonstrate that inactivation of LATS1 or LATS2, two well-characterized inhibitors of YAP1/TAZ, also decreased expression of differentiation genes in unstimulated cells but did not induce canonical YAP1/TAZ targets (Figure 4E–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E-I.

claim: PTPN14 acts through YAP1/TAZ to regulate differentiation in keratinocytes.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that PTPN14 acts through YAP1/TAZ to regulate differentiation in keratinocytes.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: It is so far unclear why CTGF and CYR61 expression is sensitive to large changes in total levels of YAP1 or TAZ yet is unaffected by alterations in regulators upstream of YAP1/TAZ.
source: It is so far unclear why CTGF and CYR61 expression is sensitive to large changes in total levels of YAP1 or TAZ yet is unaffected by alterations in regulators upstream of YAP1/TAZ.
evidence: Statement acknowledging an unexplained observation.

claim: PTPN14 knockout and knockdown reduced differentiation gene expression in monolayer culture.
source: PTPN14 knockout and knockdown reduced differentiation gene expression in monolayer culture.
evidence: Based on previous observations by the authors.

claim: We did not observe reduced differentiation in suprabasal layers of organotypic cultures grown from PTPN14 knockout cells.
source: Even so, we did not observe reduced differentiation in suprabasal layers of organotypic cultures grown from PTPN14 knockout cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HPV18 E7 promotes basal cell retention.
source: Using our cell fate monitoring assay, we determined that instead, HPV18 E7 promotes basal cell retention and that either YAP1 overexpression or PTPN14 KO is sufficient for this activity (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Either YAP1 overexpression or PTPN14 KO is sufficient for basal cell retention.
source: Using our cell fate monitoring assay, we determined that instead, HPV18 E7 promotes basal cell retention and that either YAP1 overexpression or PTPN14 KO is sufficient for this activity (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The HPV18 E7 R84S mutant that cannot degrade PTPN14 was impaired, but not completely deficient, in its ability to promote basal cell retention.
source: The HPV18 E7 R84S mutant that cannot degrade PTPN14 was impaired, but not completely deficient, in its ability to promote basal cell retention.
evidence: Supported by cell fate monitoring data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: E7 activities in addition to PTPN14 degradation might contribute to basal cell retention.
source: We interpret these data to mean that E7 activities in addition to PTPN14 degradation might contribute to basal cell retention.
evidence: Interpretation of the partial activity of the R84S mutant.

claim: GFP-labeled basal cells in the HPV18 E7 R84S cell fate monitoring experiments were present in clusters, suggesting that cells that were able to remain in the basal layer had undergone clonal expansion.
source: GFP-labeled basal cells in the HPV18 E7 R84S cell fate monitoring experiments were present in clusters, suggesting that cells that were able to remain in the basal layer had undergone clonal expansion.
evidence: Observation and inference from immunofluorescence images.

claim: It is possible that RB1 inactivation by the mutant E7 drives an apparent increase in R84S mutant basal cells in this assay.
source: It is possible that RB1 inactivation by the mutant E7 drives an apparent increase in R84S mutant basal cells in this assay.
evidence: Speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed phenotype.

claim: The effect of YAP1 activation on cell fate in our assay resembles several experiments in which YAP1 promotes progenitor cell identity in airway and liver epithelia.
source: The effect of YAP1 activation on cell fate in our assay resembles several experiments in which YAP1 promotes progenitor cell identity in airway and liver epithelia (Yimlamai et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to published research in other tissue types.

claim: YAP1 activation enables basal cell fate determination in stratified squamous epithelia.
source: Our findings demonstrate that YAP1 activation enables basal cell fate determination in stratified squamous epithelia and show that loss of an inhibitor of YAP1 has the same effect.
evidence: Conclusion based on cell fate monitoring experiments.

claim: Loss of an inhibitor of YAP1 enables basal cell fate determination in stratified squamous epithelia.
source: Our findings demonstrate that YAP1 activation enables basal cell fate determination in stratified squamous epithelia and show that loss of an inhibitor of YAP1 has the same effect.
evidence: Conclusion based on cell fate monitoring experiments.

claim: One consequence of YAP1 activation by HPV E7 is that E7-expressing cells are retained in the basal layer of stratified squamous epithelia.
source: We conclude that one consequence of YAP1 activation by HPV E7 is that E7-expressing cells are retained in the basal layer of stratified squamous epithelia.
evidence: Conclusion based on cell fate monitoring experiments.

claim: Persistent infection is a prerequisite for HPV-mediated carcinogenesis.
source: Although persistent infection is a prerequisite for HPV-mediated carcinogenesis, the mechanisms used by papillomaviruses to establish persistent infections remain incompletely understood.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of HPV biology.

claim: The mechanisms used by papillomaviruses to establish persistent infections remain incompletely understood.
source: Although persistent infection is a prerequisite for HPV-mediated carcinogenesis, the mechanisms used by papillomaviruses to establish persistent infections remain incompletely understood.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Maintaining infection in the basal cell compartment is critical for papillomavirus persistence.
source: Maintaining infection in the basal cell compartment is critical for papillomavirus persistence.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of HPV biology.

claim: Substantial effort has been devoted to the mechanistic understanding of how the papillomavirus genome is stably maintained in the basal layer upon cell division.
source: Substantial effort has been devoted to the mechanistic understanding of how the papillomavirus genome is stably maintained in the basal layer upon cell division.
evidence: Statement about the focus of previous research.

claim: Much less is known about how papillomaviruses manipulate epithelial cell fate to establish and expand the pool of infected basal cells.
source: However, much less is known about how papillomaviruses manipulate epithelial cell fate to establish and expand the pool of infected basal cells.
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: HPV E7 was believed to be primarily required to establish a cellular environment conducive to HPV DNA replication in suprabasal cells.
source: Previously, HPV E7 was believed to be primarily required to establish a cellular environment conducive to HPV DNA replication in suprabasal cells (Cheng et al., 1995; Collins et al., 2005; Flores et al., 2000; McLaughlin-Drubin et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement about previous understanding, supported by citations.

claim: A so far unappreciated role of E7 is that it activates YAP1 to facilitate HPV persistence by biasing infected cells to remain in the basal layer of the epithelium.
source: We propose that a so far unappreciated role of E7 is that it activates YAP1 to facilitate HPV persistence by biasing infected cells to remain in the basal layer of the epithelium.
evidence: Proposed conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Not every HPV E7-expressing cell was retained in the basal layer.
source: Not every HPV E7-expressing cell was retained in the basal layer, so we do not anticipate that YAP1 activation would block differentiation-dependent HPV replication.
evidence: Observation from cell fate monitoring experiments.

claim: We do not anticipate that YAP1 activation would block differentiation-dependent HPV replication.
source: Not every HPV E7-expressing cell was retained in the basal layer, so we do not anticipate that YAP1 activation would block differentiation-dependent HPV replication.
evidence: Inference based on the incomplete retention of E7-expressing cells in the basal layer.

claim: HPV E6 also represses differentiation gene expression in keratinocytes and has been proposed to promote basal cell retention.
source: HPV E6 also represses differentiation gene expression in keratinocytes and has been proposed to promote basal cell retention (Kranjec et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kranjec et al., 2017.

claim: Further research is needed to determine the extent to which different HPV genotypes depend on the activities of E6 or E7 for basal cell retention activity.
source: Further research is needed to determine the extent to which different HPV genotypes depend on the activities of E6 or E7 for basal cell retention activity.
evidence: Statement about future research directions.

claim: No other viruses are recognized to modulate cell fate decisions in solid tissues in a way that facilitates persistence.
source: To the best of our knowledge, no other viruses are recognized to modulate cell fate decisions in solid tissues in a way that facilitates persistence.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the findings in the context of virology.

claim: Some herpesviruses impact the choice between progenitor/differentiated cell fates in infected immune cells.
source: Some herpesviruses impact the choice between progenitor/differentiated cell fates in infected immune cells, for example Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and human herpesvirus 6B (HHV6B) restrict differentiation in infected cells (Knox and Carrigan, 1992; Niiya et al., 2006; Onnis et al., 2012; Romeo et al., 2019; Styles et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Herpesviruses, polyomaviruses, and hepadnaviruses encode proteins proposed to activate YAP1/TAZ or alter Hippo signaling.
source: Herpesviruses, polyomaviruses, and hepadnaviruses encode proteins proposed to activate YAP1/TAZ or alter Hippo signaling (Hwang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015a; Liu et al., 2015b; Nguyen et al., 2014; Shanzer et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Not all of the mechanisms used by these viruses to activate YAP1 nor the downstream consequences of YAP1 activation have been well defined.
source: Not all of the mechanisms used by these viruses to activate YAP1 nor the downstream consequences of YAP1 activation have been well defined.
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: HPV E7 activates YAP1 to manipulate cell fate.
source: Our finding that HPV E7 activates YAP1 to manipulate cell fate opens up an exciting new line of inquiry into how YAP1, TAZ, and the Hippo signaling pathway could impact viral infections by regulating tissue developmental processes.
evidence: Conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: YAP1 activation and PTPN14 are relevant to both viral and nonviral cancers.
source: YAP1 activation and PTPN14 are relevant to both viral and nonviral cancers.
evidence: Statement introducing the broader relevance of the findings.

claim: A genetically encoded inhibitor of YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcription inhibited the growth of high-risk HPV E7 expressing cells.
source: We found that a genetically encoded inhibitor of YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcription inhibited the growth of high-risk HPV E7 expressing cells (Figure 6), indicating that high-risk HPV E7 proteins require YAP1 or TAZ for carcinogenesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: High-risk HPV E7 proteins require YAP1 or TAZ for carcinogenesis.
source: We found that a genetically encoded inhibitor of YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcription inhibited the growth of high-risk HPV E7 expressing cells (Figure 6), indicating that high-risk HPV E7 proteins require YAP1 or TAZ for carcinogenesis.
evidence: Conclusion based on TEADi inhibitor experiments.

claim: YAP1/TAZ activation is sufficient to drive carcinogenesis in mouse models of cervical and oral cancer.
source: YAP1/TAZ activation is sufficient to drive carcinogenesis in mouse models of cervical and oral cancer (He et al., 2019; Nishio et al., 2020; Omori et al., 2020), and the YAP1 inhibitor verteporfin reduced the growth of HPV-positive tumors in a xenograft model (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: The YAP1 inhibitor verteporfin reduced the growth of HPV-positive tumors in a xenograft model.
source: YAP1/TAZ activation is sufficient to drive carcinogenesis in mouse models of cervical and oral cancer (He et al., 2019; Nishio et al., 2020; Omori et al., 2020), and the YAP1 inhibitor verteporfin reduced the growth of HPV-positive tumors in a xenograft model (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: YAP1 activation correlates with the clinical stage of HPV infection.
source: YAP1 activation correlates with the clinical stage of HPV infection (Nishio et al., 2020), and YAP1 localizes to the nucleus in HPV-positive cancers (Alzahrani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nishio et al., 2020.

claim: YAP1 localizes to the nucleus in HPV-positive cancers.
source: YAP1 activation correlates with the clinical stage of HPV infection (Nishio et al., 2020), and YAP1 localizes to the nucleus in HPV-positive cancers (Alzahrani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alzahrani et al., 2017.

claim: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the nonviral cancer that is most clearly linked to PTPN14.
source: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the nonviral cancer that is most clearly linked to PTPN14.
evidence: Statement based on the following evidence about PTPN14 and BCC.

claim: Germline inactivating mutations in PTPN14 are associated with a fourfold to eightfold increase in risk of BCC by age 70.
source: Germline inactivating mutations in PTPN14 are associated with a fourfold to eightfold increase in risk of BCC by age 70 (Olafsdottir et al., 2021) and somatic mutations in PTPN14 are frequent in BCC (Bonilla et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olafsdottir et al., 2021.

claim: Somatic mutations in PTPN14 are frequent in BCC.
source: Germline inactivating mutations in PTPN14 are associated with a fourfold to eightfold increase in risk of BCC by age 70 (Olafsdottir et al., 2021) and somatic mutations in PTPN14 are frequent in BCC (Bonilla et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bonilla et al., 2016.

claim: YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity restricts differentiation in BCC cells.
source: YAP1/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional activity also restricts differentiation in BCC cells (Yuan et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yuan et al., 2021.

claim: The specific association of PTPN14 with BCC is related to the observation that PTPN14 loss activates YAP1 in basal epithelial cells.
source: We propose that the specific association of PTPN14 with BCC is related to our observation that PTPN14 loss activates YAP1 in basal epithelial cells.
evidence: Proposed conclusion connecting the experimental findings to BCC biology.
